etymology: From the Greek psalmos, a song sung to the harp, rendering the Hebrew mizmor; the number marks its place in the Psalter, the longest chapter in Scripture.
biblical_def: Psalm 119 is the great acrostic psalm in praise of the word of God, the longest chapter in the whole of Scripture. It is built in twenty-two sections of eight verses each, following the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet, so that every verse in a section begins with the same letter—a sustained meditation wrought with deliberate artistry. Nearly every one of its hundred and seventy-six verses names the word of God under some title: the law, the testimonies, the statutes, the precepts, the commandments, the judgments, the word, the way. The psalmist confesses, "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path" (119:105), and again, "O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day" (119:97). Here is no cold legalism but the believer's delight in the revealed mind of God—the word hidden in the heart that one might not sin (119:11). This dictionary confesses with the psalmist that the Scriptures are the very breath of God, sufficient, settled forever in heaven (119:89), and the lamp by which the saint walks the whole way home.
webster_summary: The longest chapter of the Bible; an acrostic psalm of twenty-two eight-verse stanzas ordered by the Hebrew alphabet, almost every verse extolling the law and word of God. It is the believer's sustained song of delight in Scripture.
webster_full: PSALM 119, noun. The longest chapter in the sacred volume, an acrostic hymn in twenty-two stanzas of eight verses, each stanza headed by a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
Its theme is the excellency of the word of God, named under eight chief titles: law, testimonies, statutes, precepts, commandments, judgments, word, and way.
"Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path" (119:105).
It requires of the saint a settled love and meditation upon Scripture, and forbids the contempt that turns from God's commandments.
Its closing note is the lost sheep restored: "I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek thy servant" (119:176).
scriptures: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.
For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven.
O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is rather the cold heart that recites the psalm without sharing its love for the law of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief peril to this psalm is not redefinition but neglect. An age that prizes spontaneity over discipline finds an acrostic meditation on the law tedious, and an age that pits grace against law misreads the psalmist's delight as bondage. Yet the psalm refutes both: it is the cry of a man set free, who loves the commandments because he loves the God who gave them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is the believer's delight in the whole counsel of God—not the law as a ladder to merit, for that the gospel forbids, but the law written on the heart of the regenerate, who with David counts the testimonies of the LORD better than thousands of gold and silver.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew mizmor (a psalm) and the eight Hebrew nouns the psalmist heaps upon the word of God, ordered by the twenty-two letters of the alphabet.
roots_lines: Mizmor, Hebrew, a song accompanied by stringed instruments, rendered psalmos in the Greek.
The acrostic form runs the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet, eight verses to each.
Torah, law or instruction, the most frequent of the psalm's titles for the word of God.
Edoth, testimonies; chuqqim, statutes; piqqudim, precepts—the rich vocabulary of revelation.
Dabar, word, and imrah, saying, both naming the spoken and written utterance of God.
usage: The young pastor preached through Psalm 119 stanza by stanza over a year, that the people might learn to love the word.
She memorized the aleph section of Psalm 119 before she could read the Hebrew letters that ordered it.
When his faith grew cold, he returned to Psalm 119 and found his delight in the testimonies rekindled.

etymology: From the Greek psalmos, a song to the harp; this psalm bears the title Maschil of Asaph, a contemplative instruction by the chief Levitical singer.
biblical_def: Psalm 78 is the long maskil of Asaph, a psalm of instruction that rehearses the history of Israel from the bondage in Egypt to the raising up of David. Asaph opens with a solemn charge to teach: "We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done" (78:4), that the coming generations "might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments" (78:7). The body of the psalm is a sober rehearsal of God's faithfulness amid Israel's covenant unfaithfulness—the plagues, the Red Sea, the manna, the water from the rock—set against a people who "tempted and provoked the most high God, and kept not his testimonies" (78:56). Yet God remembered that they were but flesh, and at the last chose Judah, mount Zion, and David his servant. This dictionary confesses that the right use of redemptive history is catechetical: the fathers must teach the children the mighty acts of God, that hope be set on Him and not forgotten in the generations.
webster_summary: Asaph's maskil rehearsing Israel's history from Egypt to David, with a charge to teach the works of God to every generation. Its lesson is the LORD's faithfulness set against His people's repeated unfaithfulness.
webster_full: PSALM 78, noun. A maskil of Asaph, a didactic psalm rehearsing the history of Israel from the deliverance out of Egypt to the election of David.
Its opening charge is generational: the fathers are to teach the children the praises and wonderful works of the LORD.
"That the generation to come might know them, even the children which should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children" (78:6).
It requires the household to catechize its young in the mighty acts of God, and forbids the forgetfulness that breeds apostasy.
Its closing sense is grace triumphant: God chose Judah, Zion, and David, despite the rebellion of the people.
scriptures: Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Psa 78:7
That they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments:
Psa 78:5
For he established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children:
He chose David also his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the loss to recover is the household catechesis that hands the works of God down through the generations.
corruption_paragraphs: No modern framework labors to overturn Psalm 78, but the practice it commands has been widely abandoned. Where once fathers rehearsed the mighty acts of God at the family table, an age that outsources instruction to screens and to the state leaves the children ignorant of the works of the LORD. The psalm itself names the result: a generation that knew not God, that set not its heart aright, and turned back in the day of battle.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is generational faithfulness in the home—that the fathers, the heads of households under God, teach their children the redemptive acts of God, that the next generation set its hope on Him and keep His commandments.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew maskil (an instructive psalm) of Asaph, the chief of the Levitical singers appointed by David.
roots_lines: Maskil, Hebrew, a psalm of contemplation or instruction; the title of several psalms.
Asaph, a chief musician and seer appointed over the song of the house of the LORD.
The psalm follows the wilderness narrative of Exodus, Numbers, and Joshua in poetic rehearsal.
Dor, generation; the key word of the opening charge to teach the children.
Edoth, testimony, established in Jacob that the fathers might make it known.
usage: He read Psalm 78 to his sons each Lord's Day evening, that they might know the works of God.
The catechism class traced Psalm 78 alongside the books of Exodus and Numbers.
Asaph's charge in Psalm 78 shaped the church's vision for family worship.

etymology: From Latin accusare, to call to account; rendering the Greek kategor, a prosecutor in a court; brethren from Old English brothor, the saints as brothers in Christ.
biblical_def: The Accuser of the Brethren is a title of Satan, the great adversary whose office is to slander and indict the people of God. John hears in heaven a loud voice proclaiming, "Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night" (Rev 12:10). The pattern is set early: in Job, Satan presents himself before the LORD and slanders the patriarch's integrity (Job 1:9-11); in Zechariah he stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to resist him, and is rebuked, "The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan" (Zech 3:2). His Greek name diabolos means slanderer. Against this ceaseless accusation stands the believer's mighty comfort: Christ is the Advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1), and Paul asks, "Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth" (Rom 8:33). This dictionary confesses that the accusations of the devil, though often true of our sin, are silenced by the imputed righteousness of Christ, who answers every charge at the bar of God.
webster_summary: A title of Satan as the slanderer who indicts the saints before God day and night. His every accusation is answered by Christ the Advocate and the justifying verdict of the Father.
webster_full: ACCUSER OF THE BRETHREN, noun. A scriptural title of Satan, the adversary who slanders and brings charges against the people of God.
He accuses the saints before the throne day and night, as in the visions of Job, Zechariah, and the Revelation.
"The accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night" (Rev 12:10).
His office requires of the saint no self-defence but flight to the Advocate, and forbids despair under his charges.
His sentence is already pronounced: cast down, and to be cast at last into the lake of fire.
scriptures: And I heard a loud voice saying in heaven, Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night.
Job 1:9
Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, Doth Job fear God for nought?
Zech 3:1
And he shewed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him.
1 John 2:1
My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the modern denial of a personal devil, which leaves the conscience defenceless before its own accusations.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern temper, embarrassed by a personal devil, reduces the accuser to a psychological projection or an inner voice of guilt. But Scripture knows a real adversary, a created spirit fallen into malice, who stands before God to indict the saints. To deny him is not to be rid of his accusations but to be left without the doctrine that answers them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the courtroom of grace: the elect have an Advocate, and the Judge who would condemn is the very God who justifies. Whatever the accuser charges, true or false, the blood of Christ and His imputed righteousness silence the prosecution forever.
roots_summary: From the Greek kategor (accuser) and diabolos (slanderer), the legal vocabulary of Satan's office against the saints.
roots_lines: Kategor, Greek, a prosecutor or accuser, used of Satan in Revelation 12:10.
Diabolos, Greek, slanderer or false accuser, the common New Testament name for the devil.
Satan, Hebrew, the adversary, the one who opposes and resists.
Advocate, Greek parakletos, one called alongside to plead, the office of Christ for His own.
The courtroom imagery of Job, Zechariah, and Romans frames sin as a charge and grace as the verdict.
usage: When the accuser of the brethren whispered his old sins, the believer fled to the Advocate and was at peace.
The pastor preached that the accuser's charges are often true, but always answered in Christ.
Luther taught the saint to send the accuser of the brethren to the cross, where every debt is paid.

etymology: From Latin templum, a space marked out for worship; rendering the Hebrew hekal (palace, temple) and beth (house of God).
biblical_def: The doctrine of the temple traces the dwelling-place of God among His people from Solomon's house, through the second temple raised after the exile, to the temple Herod enlarged in the days of Christ. The temple was the appointed place of God's special presence and of sacrifice, where the blood of bulls and goats was offered upon the altar. Yet its types pointed beyond itself. Christ declared of His own body, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19), and John adds, "But he spake of the temple of his body" (John 2:21). In Him the true dwelling of God with man is fulfilled. And the church, united to Christ, is now the temple of God: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" (1 Cor 3:16), "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets" and growing "unto an holy temple in the Lord" (Eph 2:21). This dictionary confesses that the stone temple has served its purpose and passed away; the substance is Christ, and the Spirit-indwelt church His holy habitation.
webster_summary: The successive sanctuaries at Jerusalem—Solomon's, the second temple, and Herod's—as the place of God's dwelling and sacrifice. All are fulfilled in Christ's body and in the church as the Spirit-indwelt temple of God.
webster_full: THE TEMPLE, noun, in doctrine. The dwelling-place of God among His people, built first by Solomon, rebuilt after the exile, and enlarged by Herod.
It was the appointed seat of God's special presence and the place of sacrifice under the old covenant.
"Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. . . . But he spake of the temple of his body" (John 2:19, 21).
Its types require the believer to see them fulfilled in Christ, and forbid a return to the shadows now that the substance is come.
Its present sense is the church: a holy temple in the Lord, an habitation of God through the Spirit.
scriptures: John 2:21
But he spake of the temple of his body.
Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?
Eph 2:21
In whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord:
1 Kings 6:1

And it came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel were come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel, in the month Zif, which is the second month, that he began to build the house of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Modern errors revive a literal future temple with restored animal sacrifice; against this the doctrine confesses Christ as the temple's fulfillment, the once-for-all sacrifice never to be repeated.
corruption_paragraphs: Dispensational premillennialism, a nineteenth-century novelty after Darby and Scofield, looks for a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem with a renewed Levitical sacrifice in a coming age. This Scripture forbids. The epistle to the Hebrews declares that Christ has by one offering perfected forever them that are sanctified, and that where there is remission of sin there is no more offering for sin. To rebuild the altar is to deny the sufficiency of the cross.

The Reformers recovered the temple's true reading against Rome no less than against the literalists. The temple was a shadow, and the substance is Christ; the church is now the temple of God, indwelt by the Spirit, with no mediating priesthood but Christ and no continuing sacrifice but the praise of redeemed lips. The believer needs no holy place of stone, for God dwells in His people.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew hekal and beth (house) of the LORD, fulfilled in the Greek naos, the temple of Christ's body and of the church.
roots_lines: Hekal, Hebrew, palace or temple, the holy place of the LORD's house.
Beth, house; the temple called the house of God throughout the Old Testament.
Naos, Greek, the inner sanctuary, applied by Christ and Paul to the body and the church.
Solomon's temple, the second temple of Zerubbabel, and the temple enlarged by Herod mark the historical stages.
The veil rent at the crucifixion declared the way into the holiest now open in Christ.
usage: He taught that the temple doctrine forbids any rebuilt sanctuary with restored sacrifice, for Christ has offered Himself once for all.
The congregation learned that they themselves, gathered in Christ, are the temple of God.
Tracing the temple doctrine from Solomon to the church, the elder showed how every shadow met its substance in the Lord.

etymology: From Oxford, the English city where they suffered; martyr from Greek martys, a witness, one who seals his testimony with blood.
biblical_def: The Oxford Martyrs were Thomas Cranmer, Hugh Latimer, and Nicholas Ridley, leading bishops of the English Reformation burned at Oxford under Queen Mary I in the years 1555 and 1556. Cranmer, archbishop of Canterbury, had given the realm its Prayer Book and its homilies; Latimer was the great preacher of the gospel to king and commons; Ridley, bishop of London, was a master of the doctrine of the Supper against the Roman corruption. When Latimer and Ridley were brought to the stake together in October 1555, Latimer spoke the words that have rung down the centuries: "Be of good comfort, Master Ridley, and play the man; we shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out." Cranmer, who had recanted under pressure, repented his recantation and thrust the offending hand first into the flame. They died for the recovered gospel of justification by faith alone, against the mass and the papacy. This dictionary honors them as faithful witnesses who, like the martyrs under the altar (Rev 6:9), loved not their lives unto the death.
webster_summary: Cranmer, Latimer, and Ridley, English Reformation bishops burned at Oxford under Mary I in 1555 and 1556. Their deaths sealed the recovered gospel and kindled a witness, in Latimer's words, never to be put out.
webster_full: THE OXFORD MARTYRS, noun, plural. Thomas Cranmer, Hugh Latimer, and Nicholas Ridley, bishops of the English Reformation, burned at Oxford under Mary I.
They suffered in 1555 and 1556 for the gospel of justification by faith and against the mass and the papacy.
Latimer at the stake: "Be of good comfort, Master Ridley, and play the man; we shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out."
Their witness requires of the church a like steadfastness, and forbids the recantation that purchases life by denying Christ.
Their sense in history: the candle they lit secured the Reformed faith of England against Rome.
scriptures: Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
Acts 7:59
And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though a softened ecumenism would dismiss their deaths as needless; the witness to recover is faithfulness unto death for the recovered gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: A modern ecumenism eager to heal the breach with Rome is tempted to treat the Oxford Martyrs as victims of mere intolerance, their doctrine an unfortunate sticking-point better forgotten. But they did not die for trifles. They died for justification by faith alone against the merit of works, for the true doctrine of the Supper against transubstantiation, for the supremacy of Christ against the papacy. To minimize their cause is to despise their blood.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The witness to recover is plain: that the gospel is worth dying for, and that the candle Latimer spoke of still burns wherever the recovered truth is preached. The church honors its martyrs not by mourning their loss but by holding fast the faith for which they suffered.
roots_summary: From Oxford, the place of their burning, and the Greek martys (witness), the saint who seals his confession with his blood.
roots_lines: Martys, Greek, a witness; in the New Testament one who testifies of Christ even unto death.
Thomas Cranmer, archbishop of Canterbury, author of the Book of Common Prayer, burned 1556.
Hugh Latimer, bishop of Worcester and preacher of the Reformation, burned with Ridley in 1555.
Nicholas Ridley, bishop of London, defender of the Reformed doctrine of the Supper, burned 1555.
Foxe's Acts and Monuments preserved their testimony for the comfort of the English church.
usage: He visited the memorial at Oxford where the martyrs were burned and read Latimer's dying words aloud.
The Oxford Martyrs are held up in catechesis as examples of faithfulness unto death.
When pressed to soften his confession, the young minister remembered the Oxford Martyrs and stood fast.

etymology: From Latin, the language of the Western church; father from Latin pater, applied to the early teachers who handed down the apostolic faith.
biblical_def: The Latin Fathers were the early Christian writers of the Western, Latin-speaking church, chiefly Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, Jerome, and above all Augustine of Hippo. To them the church owes a great debt under God. Tertullian gave the Latin vocabulary of the Trinity; Ambrose defended the deity of Christ against the Arians and baptized Augustine; Jerome rendered the Scriptures into the Latin Vulgate; and Augustine, the greatest of them, set forth the doctrines of original sin, sovereign grace, and predestination that the Reformers would later prize as their own inheritance. Calvin cited Augustine more than any other father. Yet they were men, not the apostles; and where they erred the church must say so. Their reverence for tradition, their early notions of baptismal regeneration, and their developing views of the church and the sacraments became seedbeds upon which a later Rome built corruptions the apostles never taught. This dictionary honors the Latin Fathers for guarding Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy and for Augustine's doctrine of grace, while measuring all they wrote by the rule of Scripture, the only infallible standard.
webster_summary: The early Western theologians—Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, Jerome, and chiefly Augustine—who guarded Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy and, in Augustine, the doctrine of grace. The Reformers honored their contributions while measuring all by Scripture.
webster_full: THE LATIN FATHERS, noun, plural. The early Christian writers of the Western church, foremost among them Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine.
They defended the Trinity and the deity of Christ, and in Augustine set forth the doctrines of original sin and sovereign grace.
"By grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God" (Eph 2:8), the truth Augustine recovered against Pelagius.
Their writings require the reverence due to faithful teachers, yet forbid the place of an infallible rule, which Scripture alone holds.
Their sense in history: a foundation of orthodoxy upon which Rome later raised corruptions the Reformers had to remove.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Acts 17:11
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: Rome appeals to the Latin Fathers to underwrite later corruptions; against this the doctrine honors their genuine contributions yet subjects them to Scripture, the sole infallible rule.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome appeals to the Latin Fathers to justify doctrines the apostles never taught—the sacrifice of the mass, baptismal regeneration as a settled dogma, prayers for the dead, the swelling authority of the bishop of Rome—as though development from a father's seedling word were equal to the word of God. But the fathers themselves bowed to the Scriptures. Augustine wrote that he gave to the canonical books alone the honor of believing they could not err, and to all others only the deference due to fallible men.

The Reformation was no rejection of the fathers but a return to their own rule. Calvin and the Reformers claimed Augustine's doctrine of grace against the medieval church that had buried it, and read the fathers as helpful servants, never as masters over Scripture. The error is not to value the Latin Fathers but to lift them to an authority they themselves disclaimed.
roots_summary: From Latin, the tongue of the Western church, and the title pater (father) given the early teachers who handed down the faith once delivered.
roots_lines: Tertullian of Carthage, who first wrought the Latin language of the Trinity, trinitas and persona.
Cyprian of Carthage, bishop and martyr, who wrote on the unity of the church.
Ambrose of Milan, who withstood the Arians and instructed the young Augustine.
Jerome, the scholar who translated the Scriptures into the Latin Vulgate.
Augustine of Hippo, doctor of grace, whose Confessions and anti-Pelagian works the Reformers prized.
usage: The seminary course on the Latin Fathers began with Tertullian and ended with Augustine.
He showed how the Reformers claimed the Latin Fathers, especially Augustine, against the church of Rome.
Reading the Latin Fathers, she learned to honor their wisdom without granting them the authority of Scripture.

etymology: From Jacob, Hebrew Yaaqob, supplanter; wrestling from Old English wraestlian, to strive hand to hand; the place named Peniel, the face of God.
biblical_def: Jacob's Wrestling is the night-long struggle at Peniel recorded in Genesis 32, on the eve of Jacob's dreaded meeting with his brother Esau. "And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day" (Gen 32:24). The man was no mere angel but a theophany, the Angel of the LORD, the preincarnate Son of God; for Jacob says, "I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved" (32:30), and names the place Peniel, the face of God. The wrestling was real and bodily, yet it was also prevailing prayer: clinging, Jacob cries, "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me" (32:26). He is given a new name, Israel, "for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed." Yet the LORD touches the hollow of his thigh, and Jacob goes forth blessed but halting. This dictionary confesses the lesson of Peniel: that the saint prevails with God not by strength but by clinging in weakness, and that those whom God most blesses He first humbles, sending them out leaning the rest of their days.
webster_summary: Jacob's night struggle at Peniel with the Angel of the LORD, a theophany of the preincarnate Son; he prevails by clinging in prayer, is renamed Israel, and is left blessed but lame. It is the pattern of prevailing prayer and the humbled saint.
webster_full: JACOB'S WRESTLING, noun. The night-long struggle of Jacob with a divine man at Peniel, on the eve of meeting Esau.
The man was the Angel of the LORD, a theophany of the preincarnate Son, with whom Jacob saw God face to face.
"I will not let thee go, except thou bless me" (Gen 32:26).
It requires of the saint a clinging, prevailing prayer, and forbids the self-reliance that walks upright in its own strength.
Its closing sense is the shrunken thigh: Jacob goes forth blessed, renamed Israel, yet halting upon his thigh.
scriptures: And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day.
And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.
And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.
And Jacob called the name of the place Peniel: for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the truth to recover is the theophany of the preincarnate Son and the pattern of prevailing, clinging prayer through humbling.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical readers reduce the wrestling at Peniel to a folk legend or an inner psychological conflict, stripping away the theophany and the new name. But the text presents a real encounter with the living God, and Jacob's own confession—that he saw God face to face—forbids the reduction. The Angel who wrestled and blessed and renamed is the same Lord who would take flesh and dwell among us.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold. First, the man at Peniel is a Christophany, the preincarnate Son made visible to the patriarch. Second, Jacob's clinging is the pattern of prevailing prayer: the saint prevails not by might but by holding fast in weakness, and the God who blesses him first lames him, that he might lean on grace and not on himself.
roots_summary: From Peniel (the face of God), the place Jacob named, and the new name Israel, he who strives or has power with God.
roots_lines: Yaaqob, Jacob, the supplanter, who took the heel of his brother at birth.
Peniel or Penuel, the face of God, the name Jacob gave the place of the struggle.
Yisrael, Israel, interpreted as a prince having power with God, or one who strives with God.
The Angel of the LORD, a theophany of the preincarnate Son who appears throughout the patriarchal histories.
The hollow of the thigh touched out of joint, the mark of the humbled and prevailing saint.
usage: He preached on Jacob's Wrestling to teach the church the meaning of prevailing prayer.
Like Jacob at Peniel, she would not let go until the blessing came.
The doctrine of the Angel of the LORD was drawn in part from Jacob's Wrestling, where the patriarch saw God face to face.

etymology: From Old English regnboga, rain-bow; the Hebrew qesheth, a bow, the same word used of the weapon of war, here set down in token of peace.
biblical_def: The Rainbow is the bow set in the cloud, the appointed token of the covenant God made with Noah and with all flesh after the flood. "I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth" (Gen 9:13). The Hebrew word is the word for a bow of war, yet here the bow is unstrung and turned upward, a weapon laid aside—God's pledge that He will never again destroy the earth by the waters of a flood. As often as the bow appears in the clouds, God says, He will remember His everlasting covenant (9:16). It is therefore a sign of His covenant faithfulness and of His common-grace preservation of a guilty world. The same bow encircles the throne of God in glory: "and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald" (Rev 4:3). This dictionary confesses the rainbow as a divine token of mercy and faithfulness; and it notes honestly the modern co-opting of the rainbow as a banner for what Scripture calls sin, and labors to recover the bow as God's own covenant sign, not man's emblem of rebellion.
webster_summary: The bow set in the cloud as the token of the Noahic covenant, God's pledge never again to drown the earth by flood; the same bow rings the throne in glory. It is a sign of covenant faithfulness and common-grace preservation.
webster_full: THE RAINBOW, noun. The arc of color in the cloud, appointed by God as the token of His covenant with Noah and all flesh.
The Hebrew names a bow of war, here laid aside as a pledge of peace between God and the earth.
"I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth" (Gen 9:13).
It requires of man the remembrance of God's faithfulness and forbids the despair that fears another universal flood.
Its highest sense is the bow round about the throne, the token of mercy in the very presence of judgment.
scriptures: Gen 9:13
I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth.
Gen 9:16
And the bow shall be in the cloud; and I will look upon it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is upon the earth.
Gen 9:12
And God said, This is the token of the covenant which I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for perpetual generations:
Rev 4:3
And he that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone: and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald.
corruption_summary: The rainbow has been co-opted in the modern age as a banner for what Scripture names as sin; the doctrine recovers it as God's own covenant token of mercy and faithfulness.
corruption_paragraphs: In the present age the rainbow has been seized by the progressive movement as the emblem of pride and of sexual identities and practices that Scripture plainly names as sin. The bow that God set in the cloud as a pledge of His faithfulness has been turned into a banner of human rebellion, waved precisely against the moral order the covenant God upholds. This is a theft and an inversion: the sign of divine mercy made the standard of defiance.

The church recovers the rainbow by remembering whose bow it is. It was God who set it, God who reads it, God who remembers His covenant when it appears. The bow is unstrung and aimed upward, the arrow of judgment withheld—a mercy, not a license. To recover the sign is to confess that the One who spared the world from flood will yet judge it by fire, and that His patience now is the space He gives for repentance, not for pride.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew qesheth, a bow of war here laid aside as a token of peace, the sign of the Noahic covenant.
roots_lines: Qesheth, Hebrew, a bow; the same word for the weapon of war, here turned to a token of mercy.
Regnboga, Old English, rain-bow, the arc of color appearing after rain.
Oth, Hebrew, a sign or token, as the rainbow is the token of the covenant.
The Noahic covenant, made with Noah and all flesh, of which the bow is the perpetual sign.
The bow about the throne in Revelation, the token of mercy set in the place of judgment.
usage: He taught his children that the rainbow is God's covenant token, not the world's banner of pride.
When the storm passed and the rainbow appeared, she remembered the covenant God made with Noah.
The pastor reclaimed the rainbow from its modern co-opting, preaching it as the sign of mercy and faithfulness.

etymology: From Latin trans, across or beyond, and Jordan, the river; the land lying beyond, that is east of, the Jordan; in Hebrew ever ha-Yarden, the side of the Jordan.
biblical_def: Transjordan is the region lying east of the river Jordan, the inheritance granted to the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh. When Israel came up out of the wilderness, these tribes, having much cattle, saw that the land of Jazer and the land of Gilead were good for cattle, and asked Moses for their portion on the eastern side rather than across the river (Num 32:1-5). Moses granted it on the condition that their armed men cross over and fight for their brethren until the western conquest was complete (Num 32:20-22). The region embraced Gilead and Bashan, the high pastures and the kingdoms of Sihon and Og. After the conquest, as the eastern tribes returned home, they built a great altar by the Jordan; the western tribes feared apostasy and gathered for war, but the altar proved to be a witness, named Ed, that the eastern tribes had part in the LORD (Josh 22:34). This dictionary confesses that the land and its boundaries were the LORD's allotment, and that the altar of witness teaches the unity of the covenant people across every dividing river.
webster_summary: The region east of the Jordan, the inheritance of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, embracing Gilead and Bashan. It is the home of the eastern tribes and of the altar of witness named Ed.
webster_full: TRANSJORDAN, noun. The territory lying east of the river Jordan, beyond the river from the land of Canaan proper.
It was given to Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and embraced the regions of Gilead and Bashan.
"The land which the LORD smote before the congregation of Israel, is a land for cattle, and thy servants have cattle" (Num 32:4).
Its grant required the eastern tribes to cross over armed and fight for their brethren, and forbade them to settle until the conquest was done.
Its closing sense is the altar Ed, a witness that the eastern tribes shared in the LORD with all Israel.
scriptures: Num 32:1
Now the children of Reuben and the children of Gad had a very great multitude of cattle: and when they saw the land of Jazer, and the land of Gilead, that, behold, the place was a place for cattle;

And Moses gave unto them, even to the children of Gad, and to the children of Reuben, and unto half the tribe of Manasseh the son of Joseph, the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, and the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, the land, with the cities thereof in the coasts, even the cities of the country round about.
Josh 22:10

And when they came unto the borders of Jordan, that are in the land of Canaan, the children of Reuben and the children of Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh built there an altar by Jordan, a great altar to see to.
Josh 22:34
And the children of Reuben and the children of Gad called the altar Ed: for it shall be a witness between us that the LORD is God.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the truth to recover is the LORD's sovereign allotment of the land and the unity of His people across every dividing boundary.
corruption_paragraphs: Transjordan draws little modern controversy of doctrine, though critical readers treat the tribal allotments as late inventions read back into an idealized past. Scripture presents them as the real grant of Moses and the real conquest under Joshua, the LORD apportioning the inheritance as He had sworn to the fathers. The boundaries east of the Jordan were no less His gift than those to the west.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the unity of the covenant people. The eastern tribes, separated by the river, feared they might be cut off from the LORD's portion; the altar named Ed answered that fear, a witness that those across the Jordan shared in the same God and the same covenant. No river divides the people whom God has joined in His covenant.
roots_summary: From Latin trans (across) and Jordan, the land east of the river; in Hebrew the side or region beyond the Jordan.
roots_lines: Trans, Latin, across or beyond, prefixed to the name of the river.
Yarden, the Jordan, the river descending from the north into the Salt Sea.
Gilead, the mountainous and well-watered region east of the river, good for cattle.
Bashan, the fertile northern land, the kingdom of Og, given to the half-tribe of Manasseh.
Ed, the altar of witness, declaring that the eastern tribes had part in the LORD.
usage: The half-tribe of Manasseh received its inheritance in Transjordan, among the heights of Bashan.
He traced the boundaries of Transjordan from Gilead in the south to Bashan in the north.
The altar of witness in Transjordan kept the eastern tribes joined to the worship of the LORD.

etymology: From Philippi, the Macedonian city to whose church Paul wrote; the passage long called the Christ Hymn for its exalted, measured praise of the Son's humbling and exaltation.
biblical_def: Philippians 2, in verses five through eleven, sets forth the mind of Christ in His self-humbling and exaltation, the passage often called the Christ Hymn. Paul exhorts, "Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus" (2:5), and then describes that mind: though He was "in the form of God," He "made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men" (2:7); He humbled Himself and "became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" (2:8). Then comes the great reversal: "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow" (2:9-10). The passage is the deep well of humility and the high tower of Christ's glory. This dictionary affirms, against the kenotic heresy, that in His humbling the Son did not divest Himself of His deity or its attributes; He emptied Himself not by subtraction but by addition, veiling His glory and taking the form of a servant, true God and true man in one person forever.
webster_summary: Paul's great passage on the mind of Christ—His self-humbling to the death of the cross and His exaltation to the name above every name. It teaches humility and affirms, against kenotic error, that the Son veiled but never surrendered His deity.
webster_full: PHILIPPIANS 2, noun. The passage in Paul's epistle, verses five through eleven, setting forth the humbling and exaltation of Christ, called the Christ Hymn.
It urges the mind of Christ upon the saints: lowliness, the esteeming of others, and self-forgetful service.
"Made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men" (2:7).
It requires the humility of Christ in His people and forbids the kenotic error that He laid aside His Godhead.
Its closing sense is universal homage: every knee shall bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.
scriptures: Phil 2:5
Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus:
Phil 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
Phil 2:8
And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
Phil 2:9
Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:
corruption_summary: The kenotic heresy reads the self-emptying as a surrender of deity or its attributes; against this the doctrine confesses that the Son veiled His glory and took a servant's form without ceasing to be fully God.
corruption_paragraphs: The kenotic heresy, arising in the nineteenth century, seized upon the words "made himself of no reputation"—in the Greek, emptied himself—to teach that in the incarnation the Son laid aside His divine attributes, His omniscience or omnipotence, becoming for a time less than fully God. This Scripture and the creeds forbid. The Son cannot cease to be what He eternally and immutably is; God does not change. To empty deity of its attributes is to deny the very Godhead it claims to honor.

The text itself supplies the true sense. The emptying is not by subtraction but by addition: the Son who was in the form of God took the form of a servant, adding to His person a true human nature while remaining true God. He veiled His glory; He did not surrender it. So the church confesses, with Chalcedon, one person in two natures, the deity unchanged and the manhood real—and at the last every knee bows to the God-man exalted.
roots_summary: From Philippi, the city of the church addressed, and the Greek kenoo, to empty, rendered "made himself of no reputation."
roots_lines: Philippi, the Roman colony in Macedonia where Paul founded the church of the Philippians.
Morphe, Greek, form; the Son was in the form of God and took the form of a servant.
Kenoo, Greek, to empty; the verb behind "made himself of no reputation," misread by the kenotic heresy.
Doulos, Greek, a bondservant; the form Christ took in the likeness of men.
Kurios, Lord; the confession every tongue shall make, that Jesus Christ is Lord.
usage: He preached Philippians 2 to press the humility of Christ upon a quarreling congregation.
Against the kenotic heresy, the elder showed from Philippians 2 that the Son veiled but never lost His deity.
The Christ Hymn of Philippians 2 was sung in the early church and confessed by the creeds.
